Title: Right. Then. Let's ban Succubus Club!

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Fred wrote:
>>You haven't been around for some of the threads in the past couple
months. There's been some experimenting with changing the way people
qualify for the finals to make victory points the first level tie-
breaker and awards finals position based on games won. This would
provide a very distinct disincentive for anyone to agree to accept
only 2 VPs and voluntarily give an opponent 3 VPs as long as they
have any reasonable chance of winning the game outright on their own.
So something can and should be done.>>

So we meet again. Only *this* time as allies!

So yeah, the whole Succubus Club deal. I decided to start a thread with the
appropriate title so it was obvious what we were talking about.

Succubus Club. A card that should be banned from tournament play. Yes. Banned.
Not because it is too powerful. Not because it is "broken". Not because it is
the key to an abusive combo. Succubus Club should be banned simply because it
allows for simply too much outside of game action to be imposed on the game--it
makes deal making too seductive and often too lucrative, and gives way too
concrete of a payoff to what in all other circumstances is a nebulous advantage
at best--smack talk and deal making.

Don't get me wrong, I'm a big fan of table talk, intimidation, and deal making.
When deals are made *without* the SC, however, the results of these deals are
usually fairly open ended, have only limited immediate pay off, or deal in
minor concrete results ("Do X now, I'll do Y later..." or "If I don't Rush you,
you won't give me vote damage.") Succubus Club allows for a huge swing in pool,
cards, and resources with limited cost--just the need for you to convince
someone across the table that it is a good idea for them to give you all their
stuff for a turn in exchange for the SC and the promise that you'll do the same
on their turn. Very concrete deals providing a huge advantage to the folks who
can pull it off.

Such deals are often viewed with obvious suspicion, especially when made in a
tournament between freinds--if I am sitting across the table from a pal of
mine, and I use SC to borrow all of his vampires and locations for one turn I
will suddenly get a huge power advantage for limited risk (as I'm borrowing the
stuff from a friend of mine who I have reason to believe will live up to the
deal), and outside viewers will be hard pressed to *not* think "Collusion!
Collusion!".

At a point in this game where rules are being implimented to lessen and prevent
collusion, it seems sheer madness to keep a card in the play set that exists
simply to *enable* collusion.

Again, is it some sort of super overpowered card that is shattering play
balance? No (well in a sense), but it does have a *huge* effect on the game, it
never ceases to piss people off, it allows way too much of a concrete benefit
to nebulous smack talk, and it seems likely that soon *all* competetive decks
will contain a SC, if for no other reason than to contest the other one in
play.

Please kill this thing.

Well... now *this* way of presenting arguments should be the way discussions

With my limited knowledge of the english language as a non-native english
speaker I nevertheless try to take the counter-position on this thread. All
your points sound perfectly reasonable and persuable, so why should anyone
be tempted to oppose your point of view? I don't know, but I try... ;-)

Succubus Club - one of my most favored cards in this game - adds a dimension
of strategic depth to the game which is AFAIK unmatched by any other CCG out
there. Collusion, I often here this word when people start discussing this
card. In my ears this word has such a.... negative attitude. I usually
wouldn't call deal-making in the described manner "collusion", but simply a
"gentlemens' agreement". People on the wrong side of the deal-making
sometimes have a feeling of being treated in an unfair manner, but I have
yet to spot this. Let me try to undermine this statement with arguments.

I guess it is a legitimate move of every player in a tournament to arrange
the playing environment in a way that allows him to collect as many victory
points as possible. So deal making in general is not the problem, but
largely enforced my the way the game-mechanics were developed (votes etc.).
Deals are part of the game. But where do deals end and collusion begin?
My interpretation here: Collusion would start when the rules are broken
(please keep in mind: Rules can be bent by cards. That's the way CCGs go) in
a way that player(s) can arrange the outcome of the game no matter what
other involved players are doing. And Succubus Club does definitly not fit
this description, because there are numerous ways players can prevent
things.
- They can play Sudden Reversal if someone tries to bring SC into play.
- They can destroy the SC and even steal it.
- Sun-Tzu once said something like: "The biggest error a general can make is
to pretend to know more than his enemy." Deals involve risks. I've seen more
than one player happily lending his partner his vampires only to have them
clubbed into torpor or outright burned. Or - even worse - the Succubus Club
is destroyed before the second part of the deal can take place.
- As the card states: "Any additional terms can be established, but none are
enfoced by the rules." If you've ever seen a deal bust by a player suddenly
cross-dealing with the rest of the field is a pain for one of the partners,
especially if something has gone wrong (see the point above).

End even *if* this whole deal-making is accompanied by only "minimal risks"
(I, for instance, have never busted a deal), I cannot see a major problem
with this. After all, V:TES is a game, *a_game*. If you've ever played "The
Great Dalmuti" (another R. Garfield game, btw) you know that not every
aspect of a game is fair. ;-)
Or to put it shortly: Of course Succubus Club can be something that is
easily mistaken as unfair, but this is part of the game. Playing "Kindred
Restructure" to change the seating order in a way to steal away a
hard-earned victory point from another player is also unfair in a way, but
nevertheless part of the game. 30 Earth Melds played in the face of a
predator desperatly trying to bleed you is also frustrating for your
predator, but part of the game.

Again: If Succubus Club would change the playing environment in a way that
noone can escape the consequences, no matter how hard he tries and what deck
he plays, then I would agree with your points. But since SC can easily be
"outmaneuvered", I cannot agree with the proposition of banning this card.

Vampirically yours,

Sascha

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija

Sascha wrote:
>>Again: If Succubus Club would change the playing environment in a way that
noone can escape the consequences, no matter how hard he tries and what deck
he plays, then I would agree with your points. But since SC can easily be
"outmaneuvered", I cannot agree with the proposition of banning this card.>>

The "it can be outmanuvered" argument is never one that really defends the
existance of a card that is bad for the game environment. Yes, it is a unique
location master card, and suffers from all the standard counters of all
theother unique location master cards--it can be contested, stolen, Sudden
Reversaled, or burned. This doesn't make it an acceptable card, however. If
there was printed in the next expansion a unique location master called "Super
Hunting Ground" that cost 1 pool and said "During your untap phase, all of your
vampires are refilled to capacity" or something, that would not be balanced,
nor would it be an acceptable card, even though it can be contested, stolen,
SRed, or burned. Just like Succubus Club.

That a card *can* be countered doesn't necessarily make it balanced. By that
logic, *any* master card would be acceptable (even the dreaded "You Lose:
Master, 0 cost. When you play this card, your prey is automatically ousted."),
'cause you can always Sudden Reversal it.

Where you need to look is not "can this card be countered somehow" (they all
can--SC can be burned; Return to Innocence could have been deflected; Madness
of the bard can be foiled by speaking only in sign language; etc.). You need to
look at "does this card have a deleterious effect on the play environment". I
(and many others) feel that SC does.

It does not ruin the game because it is too powerful, nor because it makes any
deck that plays it automatically win. It compromises the game environment
because:

A) It is free, can go in any deck in the game, and any deck can benefit from
it--there is no reason to not put one in *every* deck you ever build, as it is
always going to be useful, it is always going to help, and it is never going to
hurt having one (if for no other reason that to contest the other one at the
table).

B) Because it is free and fits in every deck, it has no actual interaction with
your in game strategy--there is no deck that will benefit any more or less than
another one from the Succubus Club. No strategy will suffer from loss of the
Succubus Club. No strategy is specifically improved by the Succubus Club. It
affects all decks equally. Thus, no reason not to include it in every deck.

C) The advantages it provides are very concrete advantages based on very
abstract concepts--deal making, that has nothing to do with your deck strategy
as a whole. Again, any deck can benefit from SC deals, no deck will suffer from
making SC deals, and no strategy won't work without SC deals.

D) The effect of the card--trading pool and cards--greatly enables questionable
game play and collusion. Yes, if you feel that SC deals are made due to
collusion, you can always complain to the judge, but it strikes me as rather
prudent to, in this time of trying to *reduce* collusiuon and "out of game
considerations" in competetive play, remove a specific card that does nothing
but encourage and reward collusion more so than any other card.

I fully realize that Succubs Club is a fun card that has a lot to offer,
entertainment wise. However, in competetive play, it greatly compromises the
play environment. If someone has a SC in play, they become the focus of the
entire game--what kind of deal can they make to win the game, who can they make
it with, how can everyone else stop them. This turns VTES from a game of
interaction between deck strategies into a game of Succubus Club. Which isn't
good.

Does SC make a deck always win? No. Is it overpowered for its cost? Possibly.
Does it greatly compromise the play environment? Yes.

Just kill the damned thing. No deck strategies are going to suffer, nothing bad
will happen if it goes away, and the competetive environment will become *much*
cleaner, easier to manage, and less vulnerable to "out of game considerations".

Messages.Body:
LSJ wrote:
>>If it gives such a huge advantage, it would've been used (abused) much more
by now than it has been.>>

It can give a huge advantage, but again, that isn't the point. The problem with
the card is that it introduces way too much of real life into the game--smack
talk and deal making gives you very concrete, quantifiable benefits ("I'll
trade you my SC for your 4 vampires and hunting ground, and on your turn we can
switch..."), giving *so* much more incentive to bring out of game
considerations into the game, and making collusion so much more lucrative. If
two players, who have decided to collude for whatever reason, are sitting
across the table from each other, there isn't really much they can do to help
each other--sure, sometimes they can give each other vote support, or maybe
they can Rush to the benifit of their ally in collusion, and rarely they can
intercept to help each other out. On the other hand, if one of them has the
Succubus Club, they can swap vampires and locations all day long--very
quantifiable, very real help to both players.

Players who know each other, even if they aren't necessarily colluding, gain
more benefit out of the SC than others. I'm more likely to make a deal with a
friend of mine, 'cause I know he'll live up to it. Thus, out of game
considerations (I know my pal, and I know how my pal will react to a SC deal)
become incredibly important with this card and the benefits (acess to trading
vampires and other cards) are so very tangible, unlike most other deals in the
game.

>>Again, if it ever actually becomes a real problem, then the problem will be
addressed. Since it has not yet been a problem, there's no reason to ban it.>>

There are countless reports of this card being a problem. People get in fist
fights because of the damned thing. People get accused of collusion becasue of
the damned thing. It is a fun card, sure, but an inappropriate one for
competetive play.

>>At NAC, I saw several decks use SC. No one complained. No one grumbled. No
mention of collusion was made.>>

Just lucky, I guess.

>>Some people grumbled about Minion Tap, however. Perhaps that card should
be banned. Then that grumbling would quietly go away.>>

Now that is just silly. Minion Tap (and any other number of powerful cards) is
hardwired into the game and the strategies involved. Countless perfectly
reasonable strategies depend on the card, and if it were removed, a large
selection of perfectly balanced deck designs would crumble away. That, and
Minion Tap does not introduce substantial out of game elements into the game
environment. Minion Tap exists solely within the confines of the game design,
and capitalizes upon the rules structure. Succubus Club, on the other hand
exists outside of the rules structure, capitalizes upon smack talk, and rewards
(very significantly--more so than any other diplomatic/political card) out of
game considerations and collusion. Minion Tap does not do this.

What deck strategy *needs* Succubus Club to exist? What deck design would cease
to be viable without Succubus club? None. No decks would suffer. No strategies
would suffer. Except those that are specifically built to capitalize upon
collusion. The negative consequences of the banning of Succubus Club in
competetive play (umm...you have a couple extra cards you can't play in a
tournament?) would be *vastly* outweighed by the positive aspects of its
removal.

Madness of the Bard was banned because it introduced too much out of game
reality into the game environment (if you aren't a native english speaker, or
have a speach disability, you will be unfairly disadvantaged by MotB). Monocle
of Clarity was banned because, as far as I can tell, it just 'caused problems
(even after the "no questions about questions" errata/clarification). Neither
of these cards were banned becasue they were too powerful or because they
showed up in too many winning decks. Succubus Club should be sitting around
having drinks with Madness of the Bard and the Monocle of Clarity.

scuppering you using it twice in a row.)

"Peter D Bakija" <pd...@aol.comANTISPAM> wrote

And this is too bad.

The insistence on the term "collusion" to regulate behavior in
V:EKN tournaments will prevent any progress in advancing
multi-player (as opposed to team) rules for this game.
As long as "collusion" is the term of rule, the requirements
for guarding against non-competitive play will be enormous.
If "collusion" is retained, there must be evidence of all
of the following:

1. A situation where two parties act in mutual benefit in a game
2. A prior relationship between the acting parties
3. Evidence that the mutual benefit violates the dynamic of
the predator - prey relationship.
4. Evidence of a previous, surreptitious arrangement bewtween
the two parties to act in such a mutual beneficial way
5. Evidence that this arrangement is fraudulent

That's just too much of a burden to be a functional rule.
Even if you discard the last requirement, it is still unlikely
that any evidence could be found to rule for collusion, barring
massive stupidity on the part of the acting parties. What's
worse, all above-the-table non-competitive behavior is
currently tolerated, given the most modest cover of
"I might not otherwise be able to achieve X victory points,"
regardless of previous relationships, conversations,
or play strategies between players (I have learned
that a statement along the lines of "I will help this
person sweep the table, since that will tie me for 2nd
with 0 VP." is acceptable in a tournament final).
In fact, the expectation that each game will yield
an average of 1 VP or 0.5 VP (among competitors of equal
skill), almost any table split will be defensible under
current rules as a VP maximizing deal (the only
requirement for any deal-making under current rules).

Unless and until V:EKN can institute rules to better
regulate the first requirement, team play will always be
advantaged, and such play between those with previous
relationships or play experience will be further advantaged.

If it doesn't already, this will eventually limit the
competitive environment, and create a barrier to
those who wish to compete in tournaments, and
will hurt the growth of this game.

- Jason Bell

CCGs. As such, it takes longer for the cards in a given set to be
thoroughly digested. It's happened several times over the years that
a card from Jyhad has been overlooked and is then used to great effect
by someone in a more recent tournament (Life Boon, Hostile Takeover,
Temptation of Greater Power, Change of Target...). In some cases, the
card isn't abuseable, but it still uncovers a new strategy in the game.
In other cases, the card is found to be abuseable and changes are made.

Speaking of Change of Target, lemme go on a rant here...For crying out
loud, if you're gonna be a big bleed deck, use Change of Target!!! I'm
sick of the bucket brigades of bleed bouncing that get created when some
jagoff recklessly flings a stealthed Govern bleed around. Quit letting
your prey use your own minions against you. Use Change of Target. Use
Spying Mission. Use Meld With the Land. Use Red Herring. I'm sick of
having to say to my cross-table buddy, "For god's sake, don't bleed!"
Change of Target has been in the game since Day One, and it's there for
a reason. Stop thinking that the only way to get a bleed to work is to
bid on eBay for a dozen Perfect Clarities.

(this rant wasn't directed at you personally...just a general rant about
the state of the game...)

At any rate, it doesn't surprise me when a card from Jyhad is overlooked.
One of the big concerns raised regarding the release schedule of new
V:TES expansions was giving players more time to digest all the cards in
each new set. One of the arguments supporting that concern was that
cards from Jyhad were overlooked and have recently been given new life.
Players didn't want to have to keep playing catch-up.
